title: 67% of Caregivers Feel Mentally Exhausted
paragraphs: Caring for our parents as they get older can be tough. And in America, while 54% of people already say they feel mentally exhausted, that figure rises to 67% among those caring for an aging family member, according to a recent survey.
Talker Research surveyed 2,000 Americans about caregiving and how being a caregiver affects them emotionally.
Caregiving is a common role: 49% of participants say they are caregivers now, 16% were caregivers in the past, and 8% plan to be one in the future.
However, among current and former caregivers, just 26% say they had expected to take on the role — and 62% say it started due to a sudden need, such as a sudden illness or accident.

And many weren't ready for it. Twenty-three percent of current and former caregivers say they were mentally unprepared for the role, while 22% say they were emotionally unprepared, and 31% say they were financially unprepared.

But these people give up a lot to care for others. Thirty-six percent say they have had to cut back on "me time" since becoming a caregiver, while 29% say their social lives have suffered. Another 27% say their own mental health is no longer a priority, while 21% say the same about their physical health.
Caregivers also have a lot of worries. Thirty-five percent worry about whether they're doing everything right, and 30% wonder if they understand the needs of the person they're caring for.
The survey asked former and current caregivers for any advice they might have.
The two most common points were the needs for patience and kindness, followed by the importance of taking time for yourself.
One survey participant said, "Find time every day for yourself, even if you have to lock yourself in the bathroom for five minutes. You can't take care of somebody else until you take care of you."
